title: Redwood technical deep dive - OOMs, CUDA timeouts & retry semantics
summary: Deep dive focused on recurrent OOMs and CUDA timeouts observed during long-context generation and batched workloads. Discussed KV cache sizing, batching heuristics, quantization tradeoffs, retry/backoff semantics, and implications for VPC/on-prem deployments. Action items: share logs + profiler traces, run targeted stress test, evaluate a conservative retry policy and KV cache limits, and follow up with an on-prem checklist and pricing estimates.
next_steps: Redwood: share raw logs + GPU profiler traces (Priya)
Customer: run stress harness with 2k seq/slot workload and send results (Samir)
Redwood: provide suggested retry/backoff policy doc and sample config (Alex)
Schedule follow-up deep dive in 1 week to review stress test outcomes (calendar invite)
action_items: Priya Desai - upload nvprof and runtime logs to shared drive by 2025-10-16
Samir Khan - run stress test with 2000 token sequences and provide traces by 2025-10-20
Alex Morgan - send security on-prem checklist and pricing ballpark by 2025-10-17
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: 75m | Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marco (Redwood SRE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Samir (Atlas Eng Lead), Nina (Atlas SRE), Leo (Atlas ML), Priya P (Atlas Security)

[00:00] Alex: hey everybody thanks for joining, uh we'll run through the root cause hunting for the OOMs and the timeouts you've been seeing — want to make sure we understand the patterns before recommending config changes. apologies in advance for any audio glitches, my a/c is loud.
[00:22] Samir: yep thanks Alex, the big thing for us is stability. we're on a mix of hosted and for some regulated flows we're testing private in our VPC. main repro is long invoices and multi-turn context, we'll hit out-of-memory a few times a day, sometimes the process just crashes or the GPU kernel times out.
[00:45] Priya (SE): quick clarifying q — when you say OOM is the host process killed or is CUDA returning an OOM error?
[00:52] Nina: it's a mix, sometimes the container gets an OOM kill, other times we see cuda runtime error: out of memory and occasionally a kernel timeout a la 700ms kernel watchdog. the traces vary.
[01:10] Priya: ok that helps. can you share the model and config? e.g. quantization, batch sizes, max sequence lengths, whether kv cache is persisted across requests?
[01:22] Leo: we're using a 70B open model (quantized to 4-bit perf), batch sizes vary 1-8 depending on client, and we keep the KV cache between messages for chat flows. max_seq for some invoices can be up to ~3k tokens.
[01:40] Marco: 3k with 70B even quantized is heavy. the KV cache grows with sequence length and can easily exhaust GPU memory if not bounded. are you using prefix compression or any offloading?
[01:54] Leo: no offload in prod, we were hoping quantization alone would be enough.
[02:01] Jordan: that's one major vector - without KV cache eviction or partial offload, long sequences will allocate large KV tensors. also batching amplifies peak memory: when two large requests are co-batched the sum pushes past capacity leading to intermittent OOM.
[02:20] Samir: right, and the strange part is it doesn't fail deterministically — sometimes same payloads succeed, other times we also see timeout errors.
[02:30] Priya: the nondeterminism is often due to scheduling and hidden fragmentation of GPU memory. CUDA's allocator doesn't always compact, so after several allocations/frees you can get fragmentation that leads to apparent OOM even if aggregate free memory would have been sufficient. kernel timeouts typically occur when a single kernel takes too long — larger batch shapes or very long seqs can cause that.
[02:51] Nina: would kernel preemption help? in our on-prem GPUs we have watchdog timers that kill long-run kernels.
[02:58] Marco: preemption is limited on many consumer GPUs; on datacenter GPUs there's more flexibility but depends on driver/runtime. workaround: cap compute per request (limit max gen length) or split generation into smaller chunks and stream.
[03:15] Samir: splitting could change semantics, we need consistent completions for invoices.
[03:22] Priya: there's a middle ground — keep full-gen semantics but do an early kv checkpoint: checkpoint the KV cache to CPU (or nvme) after certain prefix lengths and restore for continuation. that reduces GPU resident memory. downside: added latency and IO variability in VPC/on-prem.
[03:41] Leo: that's interesting, do you have benchmarks?
[03:45] Jordan: we've run internal tests — offloading KV to host RAM with async copy adds ~40-120ms per checkpoint depending on NVMe vs networked storage vs instance type. for your 95th percentile with strict SLA it might be acceptable, for low-latency flows maybe not.
[04:05] Priya: also batching heuristics: dynamic batching that groups small requests is good, but you should avoid co-batching large seq long jobs. policies: set a lightweight route classifier to keep long-seq requests single-threaded or on dedicated pool. Dedicated capacity is perfect for that.
[04:25] Samir: we do have a dedicated pool for a subset but due to cost we often fall back to shared host. sometimes fallbacks go to a different region. could region changes cause different driver versions and thus different behaviors?
[04:37] Marco: absolutely — subtle driver or CUDA runtime differences can change allocator behavior and kernel timings; also kernel code paths selected by the runtime may differ with driver/arch and cause timeouts in one environment and not another. ensure consistent runtime stack (driver + CUDA + runtime libs) across regions.
[04:54] Nina: noted. regarding retries — currently our client retries once on 5xx or timeout with exponential backoff x2 capped at 10s. sometimes we see duplicate completions in downstream systems. what's Redwood's recommendation?
[05:08] Alex: key is idempotency and safe retry semantics. for generation requests include a request_id / idempotency token. server-side Redwood supports de-dup for a short TTL; if client retries due to timeout but the server actually completed, de-dupe prevents double consumptions. we also recommend jittered exponential backoff and a short circuit on known OOM vs nonretriable errors.
[05:30] Samir: hmm in some cases the client sees a 504 but server still processed and wrote to our audit. how do we correlate?
[05:38] Priya: logs and request ids are critical — if you can capture the request_id in your client and we get the server-side trace we can correlate and tell you if the request succeeded. will help tune retry policy.
[05:50] Leo: on quantization — does int4 amplify instability? we saw better throughput but more variance in memory usage.
[05:58] Jordan: quantization reduces peak activations but can increase temporary scratch workspace needs depending on kernel selection; some optimized kernels for int4 need extra workspace which can push memory. also mixed precision kernels sometimes allocate transient buffers for dequantization. you might see more fragmentation.
[06:18] Nina: are there runtime flags we can set to reduce transient allocations?
[06:22] Priya: yes, limiting workspace size and choosing different kernel selection heuristics can help; Redwood runtime has flags to prefer memory-saver kernels at cost of a bit more compute. we can share a recommended config.
[06:34] Samir: what about retries inside the runtime — does Redwood retry when a CUDA kernel times out?
[06:42] Marco: runtime-level retries for kernel watchdogs are tricky; usually once the kernel triggers the watchdog the whole context is in a bad state. safe options: detect kernel timeout, mark instance unhealthy, drain requests to a warm standby, and retry the logical request on another instance. that avoids trying to reuse a potentially corrupted context.
[07:05] Leo: so the semantics are: client-side retry with idempotency + server-side smart placement and instance isolation?
[07:12] Alex: correct. Redwood's recommended flow: 1) client includes idempotency token; 2) server attempts once; if instance fails with a kernel timeout we mark instance unhealthy and automatically route to another instance for a single retry (server-initiated retry). we also surface a specific error code for nonretriable errors.
[07:30] Priya: and you should avoid blind client retries for errors that are likely to be nonretriable (validation, auth, malformed requests). for native timeouts you can retry but with idempotency and a limit.
[07:42] Samir: about logs — what level of traces do you need? we can supply application logs and GPU metrics but not sure about nvprof captures in prod.
[07:53] Marco: nvprof and CUPTI traces are best but for prod you can provide sampled traces from a repro environment. also include device free/used, fragmentation metrics if available, and driver versions. hiring the repro on a staging instance that mirrors prod is ideal.
[08:12] Nina: security question — if we checkpoint KV to host / nvme in our VPC, what are the encryption guarantees?
[08:20] Alex: for Private deployments Redwood supports KMS/HSM integrations and at-rest encryption for NVMe; we can provide an on-prem checklist. for hosted we encrypt snapshots with our KMS, and there are options for customer-managed keys in enterprise plans.
[08:36] Priya P (Security): we'll need SOC2 artifacts and a clear data retention policy for KV checkpoints — even ephemeral. can you include that in the checklist?
[08:44] Alex: yes we'll include retention controls and audit logs in the checklist.
[08:49] Leo: back to batching — you mentioned route-level classifiers. what's the simplest policy we can start with to avoid co-batching long requests?
[08:58] Jordan: simplest: at the router layer tag requests where max_seq > 1024 as "long" and route them to a small dedicated pool with concurrency 1-2 and batch size 1. other flows remain in shared pool with larger batching. That avoids accidental co-batching long seqs.
[09:14] Samir: cost concerns though, dedicated pools cost more. any ways to reduce cost?
[09:20] Marco: you can use dynamic bin packing: prefer running long-seq jobs on spot/dedicated cores during off-peak or run a hybrid model — keep tail-critical flows on dedicated, bulk on shared. also intelligent KV eviction lowers memory pressure enabling more jobs per GPU.
[09:35] Priya: implement an adaptive eviction policy: evict or compress old prefixes beyond X tokens, and only restore when necessary. also consider partial KV persistence to CPU instead of full checkpoint every time.
[09:46] Samir: any quick config changes we can apply to reduce OOM events now?
[09:50] Priya: yes — immediate triage steps: 1) cap per-request max_seq to 2048 temporarily; 2) reduce co-batching of large seqs by tagging routes; 3) enable memory-saver kernel preference; 4) add idempotency tokens and increase server log sampling for failed requests.
[10:06] Alex: we'll send a sample config patch with these toggles.
[10:10] Leo: about retry semantics — if the server does a single server-side retry after marking instance unhealthy, can we configure that behavior? sometimes we prefer no server retries to avoid duplicate billing.
[10:21] Jordan: yes that's configurable per-customer — server-side retry can be enabled/disabled per route; billing semantics are explicit in the SLA. we'll include that detail in the follow-up note.
[10:33] Nina: one more on kernel timeouts — we saw CUDA driver 12.x behaving differently from 11.x. any recommended driver matrix?
[10:40] Marco: we'll share recommended driver/runtime matrix. generally prefer latest stable datacenter drivers aligned with CUDA that your runtime uses; avoid mixing minor versions across fleet.
[10:49] Samir: for on-prem, would Redwood provide an agent to collect metrics?
[10:54] Alex: yes for Private we have an agent that collects GPU metrics and optional CUPTI traces; we'll share onboarding docs.
[11:02] Priya: quick note on monitoring — add alerts for fragmentation ratio and per-instance transient allocation spikes; those are leading indicators before OOM.
[11:12] Samir: solid. any gotchas with quantization and model variants?
[11:17] Jordan: model variants that enable kernel-fusion optimizations can behave differently memory-wise. we recommend profiling each variant under the same workload. quantized models are great for throughput but test stability under tail workloads.
[11:30] Alex: let's recap actions — Priya to collect logs and profiler traces, Samir to run stress harness, Alex will send config patch and security checklist, and we'll schedule a follow-up.
[11:42] Nina: sounds good. thanks team.
[11:45] Alex: thanks everyone — we'll send the notes and the config patch within 48 hours.

Notes on transcription: occasional words may be off, e.g., "nvprof" could be transcribed as "env prof" in places; speaker boundaries approximate.
